newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal hails Nobel prize for Timor rights pair.
newsitem.headline: Portugal hails Nobel prize for Timor rights pair.

text.p: Portugal reacted with delight on Friday to the award of the Nobel Peace Prize to Jose Ramos-Horta and Bishop Carlos Belo, leading defenders of human rights in East Timor, the former Portuguese colony occupied by Indonesia.
Political leaders said the award could strengthen Portugal's hand in long-running talks on the territory's future with Jakarta, whose rule has never been recognised by the United Nations.
"I am very pleased by the news. It is a wonderful surprise," President Joao Sampaio said soon after Friday's announcement by the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo.
"The award reflects their indefatigable work in the service of human rights and peace in the territory," he told reporters.
Portugal and Indonesia have been locked in a diplomatic battle ever since Jakarta invaded the territory in 1975, soon after the Portuguese left, and then annexed it a year later.
According to human rights activists, up to 200,000 people, a quarter of East Timor's population, died during the takeover and a military crackdown and famine that followed.
Tensions erupted afresh in 1991 after Indonesian troops opened fire on anti-Jakarta demonstrators in Dili, the East Timor capital, in November that year, killing around 200 people.
International outrage over the shootings led the United Nations to broker talks between Lisbon and Jakarta in 1992 aimed at reaching an agreement over the territory's future.

But four years later, the two sides remain wide apart. Indonesia, one of Asia's most populous nations, insists that East Timor is part of its country while Portugal counters that the East Timorese should be allowed to decide their own fate.

Clashes are periodically reported between a small guerrilla movement still operating in the mountains and the Indonesian army. Street demonstrations and embassy invasions by asylum seekers have kept the international spotlight on the troubled territory.

Ramos-Horta, a spokesman for the East Timor resistance movement Fretilin, told Portuguese radio that his happiness at the award was mixed with sadness that his jailed leader, Xanana Gusmao, had not also been honoured. Gusmao was sentenced to 20 years in jail after being captured in 1992.
Former Portuguese president Mario Soares echoed the words of Ramos-Horta, welcoming the joint award but saying that Gusmao should also be remembered.
Soares told a news conference in Geneva that the award was a "great encouragement for the brave and courageous people of East Timor".

Portuguese Foreign Minister Jaime Gama, who held his most recent round of talks with Indonesian counterpart Ali Alatas in June, in Switzerland, said that the award could help speed the search for a lasting accord for East Timor.
"The prize shows that the problem of East Timor needs a peaceful solution, worthy of the Nobel Prize," he told journalists.
